About the author

Lucy Foley

27 books41.8k followers
Hello and welcome to my Goodreads page! I’m the author of the new Miss Marple novel, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel. My previous books have included my murder mysteries: The Midnight Feast, The Paris Apartment, The Guest List and The Hunting Party — as well as the historical novels The Book of Lost and Found, The Invitation and Last Letter from Istanbul.

I came to writing through a love of reading — I previously worked with books as a fiction editor, a literary agent’s assistant, a bookseller and a literary scout!

Inspired by trips to the West Country and local folklore I began plotting my latest novel, The Midnight Feast. A midsummer heatwave, a setting with a past, a reunion that takes a dark turn. And so The Midnight Feast came to life.

Thanks to brilliant readers around the world, my novels have sold over five million copies, and been translated into multiple languages. I’m also a No 1 New York Times and Sunday Times bestseller. A life-long Agatha Christie fan, I also contributed to Marple, a collection of short stories featuring the legendary detective.

October 14, 2026
Well, what a pleasant surprise! You must excuse me for saying so, but I didn't think Lucy Foley had it in her.

But first things first. I think what you'll get out of this book largely depends on your expectations. Obviously, this isn't Agatha Christie's Miss Marple. How can it be? Christie was a marvel of the mystery genre, with a sharpness in writing and clarity of resolution that's hard to match, let alone imitate. But that doesn't mean someone else can't come along and borrow one of her most beloved characters and have a little fun with it. And that's exactly what Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel does.

The glorious, vintage setting, the wintry atmosphere, the effectively locked room all contribute to a murder mystery formula we know and love. The scene is set, the characters in play. What follows is what every good mystery must have—plenty of clues and twists, red herrings galore, and one dead body after another. And Miss Marple is there in the midst of the chaos, using her keen eyes and her deceptively fluffy appearance to unravel it all.

I honestly couldn't put this down once I started. I was thoroughly riveted. But was I ever confused into thinking I was reading vintage Christie there on the pages? No. Did I think Miss Marple had risen from the literary grave to laugh/knit one last time? Also no. In fact, there were many moments when I thought to myself, Miss Marple would never do or say such a thing. But for what it was—an homage to Agatha Christie with a modern twist, as well as a darn fun mystery—it did quite all right.

Everyone always wants to know about the reveal. Was it dumbfounding, gobsmacking, flabbergasting? Well, I think if you're an aficionado of the genre, I doubt you'll be taken completely unawares (and I wasn't). The story progressed in a specific way and I think you'll recognize it if you've read enough of these books. Also, in this case, the reveal lacked some of the crispness and clarity that Christie's has always been known for. But still, there were surprises to be had, and I can't complain too much when that's the case.

So back to my initial reaction for a second. I haven't had the greatest luck with Lucy Foley. She tends to favor interpersonal drama and excessive foreshadowing in her mysteries, leading to what I can only describe as anticipation fatigue and a whole lot of ado over nothing. Not to mention, this project of taking such a beloved character, as well as the seminal style of the genre, and trying to make it her own must not be easy. But clearly, I was wrong to doubt here, and I'll be the first to admit it.

At the end of the day, I think if you're a true Christie purist, this probably isn't going to cut it. It's really hard to capture the exact magic and je ne sais quoi that made the Queen of Crime so special in the first place. But if you're like me and you've read all your Agatha Christies and there's no more to be had and you'll take anything you can get, then this is well worth a gander.

"I’m glad he’s dead. Good riddance to bad rubbish.”

When I heard that Lucy Foley was writing a brand-new adventure for the legendary Miss Marple, my inner mystery nerd immediately started doing happy cartwheels across the living room. A modern thriller author tackling one of the most beloved detectives created by Agatha Christie?

Oh yes. I was absolutely ready for this literary experiment.

And I have to say it right away: Lucy Foley absolutely nailed it.

This book feels like stepping into a time machine and landing straight inside a classic Christie mystery—but with a fresh spark that makes it irresistible for modern readers. It reads like a loving tribute to Christie’s legacy, capturing the tone, the structure, and that delightful “everyone in the room is suspicious” energy that makes a proper whodunit so addictive.

The story takes us to the glamorous Grand Alpine Hotel, perched high in the Swiss Alps like the perfect postcard destination. Snow-covered mountains, elegant guests in furs and evening wear, champagne flowing, gossip drifting through the hallways… and of course the tiny little problem that someone in this luxurious paradise might be a murderer.

A blizzard isolates the hotel. Escape becomes impossible. Secrets start leaking out faster than champagne corks. And somewhere among the guests lurks a killer.

Basically, the setup is locked-room mystery heaven.

The guest list itself is deliciously suspicious. We have Catherine Narracott, the polished society wife who seems to glide through the hotel with perfect elegance. Her husband Anthony is an ambitious politician twice her age whose polished image hides more than a few cracks. Then there’s Bruno Crane—Anthony’s former wartime companion—who seems a little too startled to run into Catherine here, which immediately made my suspicious-reader radar start blinking like a Christmas tree.

And let’s not forget Sylvia Sinclair, the dazzling film star who just happens to share a rather complicated past with Anthony. Yes, that kind of past.

In other words, everyone arrives at this glamorous alpine retreat with luggage… and also emotional baggage the size of a glacier.

But the real joy of the novel is watching Miss Marple quietly observe everything while appearing to do absolutely nothing. She’s accompanied by her dear friend Mrs. Bantry and the wonderfully overwhelmed Diana Glass, who quickly realizes that being anywhere near Miss Marple means every small detail might suddenly become extremely important.

Miss Marple doesn’t storm into the investigation. She doesn’t wave clues around dramatically. Instead she does what she always does best: she watches people.

And if you’ve read enough classic mysteries, you already know that the sweet little lady with the knitting needles is probably the most dangerous mind in the building.

What I loved most about this book is how perfectly it captures the spirit of Christie’s storytelling. The pacing, the character dynamics, the slow unveiling of secrets, the carefully placed clues—it all feels wonderfully familiar in the best possible way.

At times I genuinely felt like I was reading a newly discovered Christie novel that had been tucked away in some dusty literary vault for decades.

And the setting? Absolutely perfect. The Swiss Alps add a cinematic atmosphere to the story. Snowstorms, isolated hotels, glamorous guests with hidden motives—it’s the exact kind of setting that makes a mystery reader grab snacks, settle into a cozy chair, and prepare for an evening of suspicious glances and dramatic revelations.

So yes, I happily poured myself a drink, grabbed my reading snacks, and settled in to enjoy the ride while trying (and failing) to outsmart Miss Marple.

Because let’s be honest: nobody outsmarts Miss Marple.

Overall, this was an absolute delight—a clever, atmospheric mystery that honors the traditions of classic detective fiction while introducing this iconic sleuth to a new generation of readers.

If you love traditional whodunits, glamorous settings, scandalous secrets, and brilliant elderly detectives who quietly solve crimes while everyone else is busy panicking… this one will make you ridiculously happy.

I’m giving this one five delightfully snowy mystery stars and hoping this is only the beginning of more adventures.

A very huge thanks to NetGalley and William Morrow for sharing this delicious mystery from one of my auto-approved thriller authors who captured the perfect Christie-an vibe in exchange for my honest review. I truly appreciated the opportunity to read it. 📚❄️🔎

Happy Publication Day!

I really enjoyed this one! I have a feeling it’s going to be a hit for most fans of twisty mystery/thrillers.

In Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel, a group of guests arrives at a luxurious hotel high in the Swiss Alps, each carrying secrets and old grudges. When a body is found and a blizzard cuts off all escape, Miss Marple must uncover the killer before they strike again.

I’m SO happy that this one worked for me as much as I hoped it would, especially after finding Foley’s last book, The Midnight Feast, just okay.

Lucy Foley is one of my favorite authors and is actually the person who introduced me to the genre with The Guest List. In addition to that one, I also loved The Paris Apartment. So, I went into this one with high hopes, and it didn’t take long for me to get completely invested in the story.

This story follows some very interesting characters who are all clearly hiding secrets from the start. The 1950s setting added so much to each of them, especially given the war they lived through, the way they speak, and how their backgrounds impact them as characters. I thought they were especially well done and enjoyed reading from each of their perspectives.

As someone who loves locked-room thrillers set in hotels, the Grand Alpine Hotel was the perfect setting for this book, described in amazing detail. I genuinely think this is some of Foley’s best writing.

The tone of this book is definitely more on the mystery side, though there are certainly some thrilling moments. I found this refreshing after reading so many true thrillers in a row. You really have to pay attention to the clues and try to piece everything together.

As for the twists and turns, there are multiple, and the major twist fully got me. I thought I had things figured out early on, but the story went in a direction I wasn’t expecting.

Overall, I had a great time with this one and don’t have any real complaints. The setting, characters, mystery, and twists all worked for me, and I strongly recommend checking it out!

Thank you to William Morrow for sending me an early finished copy in exchange for my honest review.

I am first and foremost an Agatha Christie fan, with Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple among my favorite characters. So, when I learned that Foley, a contemporary mystery author, was recreating Christie’s beloved sleuth, I was intrigued by the possibility of another opportunity to step into Miss Marple’s world – especially since this is the first authorized Miss Marple continuation novel in 50 years.

The biggest question of course, was this: would Foley do Madame Christie and Miss Marple justice?

“She is the very picture of a slightly dithery village spinster, prone to rambling and finding herself in confusing conversational cul-de-sacs.”

Was that a description of our very own Miss Jane Marple?

It is 1950. The Swiss Alps. A luxury resort. This is definitely not St. Mary Mead.

A murder has taken place, but readers won’t immediately know who has been killed. The story introduces readers to its characters through their own narrative voices and first-person perspectives.

Miss Marple is clearly out of her element as she takes in the scenery and settles into the winter holiday her friend and hired companion have encouraged her to join. Along with them are several other notable characters, each of whom seems to be hiding a secret of their own.

With a cast of largely unlikable characters who all seem to have something to hide – this slow-burn mystery traps its players in a treacherous, isolated environment with no way out as the danger deepens.

Will Miss Marple figure out the who and why before someone else is killed?

Foley does a reasonable job of capturing the vintage setting, post-war behaviors and classic whodunnit tension. But this is clearly not the Miss Marple readers know and love, nor does it follow the investigative storytelling style that Ms. Christie so masterfully embraced.

Readers may enjoy this as a somewhat entertaining cozy mystery filled with twists and red herrings, but for this Christie traditionalist, it simply didn’t capture the distinctive style and spirit of the original Miss Marple novels.

“There are gasps and exclamations from the nearby tables, and I hear the word repeated over and over in several different languages, the whispers dancing strangely about the room: dead... mort ... morto... tot ... miert.”

Lucy Foley was commissioned by Agatha Christie Limited to write Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel, marking the first authorized full-length Miss Marple continuation novel in 50 years.

Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel is due for release on September 22, 2026.

Foley’s ability to write the beloved detective stems from previously penning a short story for the 2022 Marple anthology, Marple: Twelve New Mysteries. This gave her a foundation to channel Christie’s iconic sleuth, though she admitted that taking on a full-length continuation was both terrifying and thrilling.

Set in the 1950s at the isolated Grand Alpine Hotel in the Swiss Alps, a glamorous winter getaway turns deadly. Cut off by a blizzard, the wealthy guests find themselves trapped with a killer. Amid the simmering grudges and champagne, only the polite and unassuming Miss Marple can unmask the murderer before they strike again.

A classic whodunnit mystery with tons of twists and turns! A super fun read sparkling with a fresh, modern edge. The setting leaps off the page, painting a vivid backdrop for the action. Written with quick, energetic momentum, the novel brings short chapters with multiple changing POVs. I think Foley channeled her skills well with this, doing absolute justice to the Queen of Crime.

I wasn't sure how Lucy Foley would handle Miss Marple on a snowy Swiss mountain in 1950, yet Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel ended up winning me over.

Marple heads to the isolated resort with her recently widowed friend, Mrs. Bantry, and a young companion named Diana Glass. Before long, a guest rides a gondola up the slope alive and arrives at the top dead—right as a storm cuts off the only train down. Foley skips Marple's internal monologue and hands the chapters over to the hotel's staff and wealthy guests. Hearing Marple snoop from the edges of someone else's scene was honestly half the fun for me.

The outsider vantage point also makes a quiet (much appreciated) point about ageism. The younger, status-obsessed crowd writes Marple off as a frail old woman who barely registers in the room, and she uses that blind spot to her advantage. People drop their guard around her in ways they never would around a detective, handing her every clue she needs. At the same time, Mrs. Bantry's grief provides readers/listeners an honest look at older women refusing to fade out just because life has changed.

Listening to the full cast audiobook made the plethora of shifting characters easy to tell apart. Even though it would have been nice if Miss Marple had a bit more plot time, the snowy, claustrophobic production made it almost impossible to pause.

Many thanks to Ms. Foley and the talented cast of narrators.

4.5 stars rounded up

It’s 1950 and Miss Jane Marple, her friend Mrs. Dolly Bantry and her ladies companion Diana Glass are aboard the Grand Alpine Express which is wending its way up the mountain to the esteemed hotel at the top. Is just as well that eagle eyed Jane Marple is a resident as the lift attendant of the gondola finds a body in it two days later… Who is the unlucky victim? As the weather worsens and the residents are stuck, Miss Marple has one tricky case to decipher.

In terms of capturing the Queen of Crime’s novels, Lucy Foley has 100% nailed it, I almost forget I’m not reading an original Christie, so huge kudos to the author for that. There’s every ingredient here for instance, it’s as if the characters have stepped straight from the 1950’s and from Agatha’s pen. There’s our eagle eyed knitter in Jane Marple who rarely misses a trick, there’s a Hollywood star, a war hero and his young wife as well as some mysterious nuns! It’s quite surreal in places which I love and there are dashes of humour.

It’s told from several perspectives just like the originals and that serves to deepen the mystery and has me casting my eye over all in order to spot any errors that they may make. Naturally, we have a “ locked room” in this case a rather grand hotel perched on a mountain with all exits closed by one means or another. The language that is used, the manners, the attitudes of society, the social mores, even down to the drinks consumed and so on, all amounts to a good bit of nostalgia from a very different age.

The plot line is classic Christie, it’s told at a brisk pace although it does slow towards the end as things start to slot into place and some good twists. The atmosphere of the snowy conditions, the smart hotel and its chilly surrounds are captured to perfection and make a great backdrop for the rising body count.

Overall, what a treat. I absolutely credit Agatha Christie with giving me a lifelong love of the mystery thriller genre and Lucy Foley has reinforced where that passion comes from. Thank you.

There’s a terrific cover too!

With thanks to NetGalley and especially to HarperCollins, HarperFiction for the much appreciated early copy in return for an honest review.

Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley is the first authorized full-length Miss Marple (created by Agatha Christie) continuation novel in decades. The setting is a resort hotel (Grand Alpine Hotel) high in the Swiss Alps above the town of St. Celeste. The year is 1950 and the hotel is only accessible by a single mountain railway. It has a classic locked-room tension after a guest enters a mountain gondola alive and turns up dead at the summit. A Blizzard cuts off the hotel and strands the guests and suspects together. Miss Jane Marple is vacationing at the resort with her longtime friend Dolly Bantry and Dolly’s paid companion, Diana Glass. She quietly observes the guests to piece together hidden secrets and motives as the body count rises.

Miss Marple has a quiet demeanor, sharp and analytical mind, and deep insight into human nature while appearing to be an unassuming elderly woman who knits. Dolly is a newly widowed aristocrat seeking a change of scenery. Diana Glass is detailed oriented and a talented photographer. There are several suspects among the quests with excellent characterization.

The author uses a style of multiple first-person narrators. While the novel is atmospheric, the writing uses an excessive number of adjectives; especially in the first half of the book which is extremely slow. In the second half, secrets and action unfold at a decent pace. Miss Marple felt like a minor character in the first part of the book, but eventually she became a central sleuth. The final twist was a little over-the-top, but not totally unexpected.

Overall, this an entertaining character-driven historical cozy mystery.

I purchased a copy of this book. All thoughts and opinions expressed in this review are my own. The publication date was September 22, 2026.

I was skeptical when this book came out. When someone tries to breathe new life into a treasured and cherished character created by another author, it can be very challenging. And Poirot’s new series by another author simply didn’t meet my expectations. So I didn’t expect to read this new Miss Marple book. But, then the reviews started coming in, and I got curious. Because a lot of my Goodreads friends enjoyed this one, with Darla’s review pushing me over the edge. So, thank you, Darla!


High in the Swiss Alps is a luxurious hotel. The hotel’s guests go up to the hotel by gondola, but one of them is found dead at the top of the mountain. So there must be a killer amongst the guests.


One big difference between Poirot and Miss Marple, in their original series, is that Poirot is always the outsider looking in, as a Belgian abroad. While Miss Marple is usually the insider. Most of the time, she is staying in her own village, where she already knows everyone. With one notable exception being A Caribbean Mystery, which I quite liked. And this story feels similar to A Caribbean Mystery for all the right reasons. Both take place at a luxury hotel, far away from Miss Marple’s comfortable and cozy village setting. In both stories, we know all the possible suspects from the start. Both stories also have a steady pace. And in both stories, Miss Marple is underestimated as she is more like a background figure for a long time.


I’m pleased to say that I enjoyed this book. It modernizes the Miss Marple series without changing the core of what a Miss Marple story is, or who she is as a character. Lucy Foley basically brings a good balance of staying true to Miss Marple’s original stories, while still adding her own touch to the series. Props in particular go to the way the other characters are written, besides Miss Marple. They really make the story for me. Just go into this book with an open mind and don’t compare it too much to the original books, and it’s a pretty good read.

I've had Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel on my radar for a while, and the combination of a glamorous Swiss hotel, a murder mystery and Miss Marple was enough to convince me to pick it up.

Set in 1950, the story takes us to the Grand Alpine Hotel, where a collection of guests have gathered for a winter getaway. Among them is Anthony Narracott, a celebrated war hero whose reputation isn't quite as impressive as he'd have everyone believe. With complicated relationships, old grudges and several reasons for certain guests to want one another out of the picture, there's no shortage of potential suspects once the first murder takes place.

Between the snow-covered mountains, the grand hotel and all the skiing excursions, it's a great location for a murder mystery. Of course, there's a lot more going on than everyone enjoying a fancy holiday in the Alps, with secrets from the war and stolen gold giving several of the characters something to worry about. The multiple perspectives also let us see sides of the guests that others aren't aware of, revealing just how unpleasant some of them really are beneath their carefully maintained appearances.

As for Miss Marple, I can see why she's such a beloved character. She's observant, sharp and unassuming, quietly taking everything in while the people around her underestimate just how much she's noticed. I enjoyed the lighter moments she shared with Mrs Bantry, whose friendship and banter brought some much-needed humour to the story. Diana was another interesting character, and her background gave her a reason to become involved in the investigation beyond simply being another guest caught up in a murder. At times, I thought the story spent a little too long on the characters' personal dramas and drawn-out conversations, and I would have preferred more focus on the actual investigation.

By the time Miss Marple began explaining everything, I was keen to see whether my suspicions were anywhere near the truth. A few things I'd noticed earlier finally made sense, while other details I'd barely thought twice about turned out to be important. However, some of the planning behind the murders was a bit of a stretch, and I couldn't help thinking how easily the whole thing could have fallen apart if even one little detail hadn't gone according to plan.

I also liked that the epilogue gave Diana's story a satisfying conclusion through her final conversation with Miss Marple, and that we got to see what happened after the events at the hotel rather than leaving everything at the big reveal.

Despite a few reservations about the pacing and how elaborate the murder plot became, I had a good time with this one. I haven't read any of Agatha Christie's original Miss Marple novels yet, but Lucy Foley's interpretation has made me even more keen to go back to the beginning and discover the character for myself.

A modern reimagining of an Agatha Christie whodunnit with Lucy Foley’s trademark edge-of-your-seat thriller flair, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel managed to captured the spirit and tone of a Miss Marple mystery while also breathing new life into it as well. You see, she not only wove together a cleverly layered web of secrets and lies, but she gave this Golden Age crime fiction novel a very The Hunting Party-like feel. With a remote snowed-in luxury setting, a locked-room mystery, and a cast of characters who started dropping like flies, the tension was high as the suspicion bounced around the side-eye-worthy suspects. Adding to the charm was a very true-to-character Miss Marple, even if she wasn’t around as much as I would’ve liked. Then again, this was somewhat inevitable given the fact that there was a round-robin volley of multiple first-person POVs in the style that Ms. Foley does so well.

I do have to say, though, that two of the best pieces to this reverent homage had to be the colorful characters and the Christie-esque 1950s atmosphere. Bringing to life the lavish and yet also claustrophobic feel of the Grand Alpine Hotel, nods to an accurate history of the time and place were included with care—along with a few Easter eggs to the OG Miss Marple stories. Rounding this off with a cast of suspicious individuals, who kept my guesses flowing, their old grudges and questionable motives added a depth to the plot that I wasn’t expecting. Miss Marple, however, was the star of the show with her perceptive shrewdness on display from the get-go. So while parts of this book didn’t quite match a classic Christie murder mystery, that was actually preferable to Foley trying her hand at what the Queen of Crime perfected years ago. Bravo, Ms. Foley, I think you knocked it out of the park. Rating of 4.5 stars.

Read if you’re a fan of:
- Agatha Christie novels
- Lucy Foley’s thrillers
- Golden Age crime fiction
- A cinematic feel
- Amateur sleuthing
- Multiple POVs
- A remote, snowed-in setting
- 1950s nostalgia
- Locked-room mysteries
- Short chapters
- Claustrophobic vibes
- Shocking twists
- Unguessable endings

SYNOPSIS:

High in the Swiss Alps, accessible only by a single, winding railway, stands the luxurious Grand Alpine Hotel. With glorious mountain views and exclusive access to powdery slopes, it draws guests from far and wide.

The notorious actress. The high-flying politician. The society wife. The reckless friend. The shrewd doctor.

But not everyone is here for a winter holiday.

Beneath the champagne and furs, dark histories simmer; old grudges emerge like cracks in the ice.

And someone is watching from the shadows. A polite, unassuming woman with an extraordinary mind: Miss Marple.

When a body is found and a blizzard cuts off all escape, only Miss Marple can connect the clues before the killer strikes again. Because it isn’t a question of who has a motive, but who’s next…

Thank you Lucy Foley and William Morrow for my complimentary copy. All opinions are my own.

Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel was, I felt, a respectful homage to Miss Marple. Foley was not trying to imitate; she wrote her usual thriller (multi-POV, first person, present tense) with a Christie-ish edge (characters, time period, dialogue).

Review of advance copy received from NetGalley
September 9, 2026
‘I find the actions of human beings are usually far more portentous of coming danger than any natural phenomenon.’

Set in a luxury hotel high in the snow-covered Swiss Alps, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel sees Lucy Foley pay homage to Agatha Christie's beloved Miss Marple - and she does so with remarkable success.

It's been a long time since I've read a Miss Marple mystery (I'm usually pro-Poirot), but Foley captures not only Miss Marple's quiet powers of observation, but also the elegance, manners and unmistakable atmosphere of the post-war era.

Miss Marple arrives at the Grand Alpine with her friend, only to find herself surrounded by a colourful cast of guests, each harbouring secrets of their own. Told through alternating viewpoints, the isolated Alpine setting provides the perfect backdrop for a locked-room mystery filled with twists, suspicion and wonderfully executed red herrings. I was convinced I'd identified the culprit more than once - only to discover I'd fallen for exactly the distractions Foley intended.

Beyond the mystery itself, Foley evokes the glamour and cosiness of a winter escape in the Swiss Alps. Crackling fires, snow-covered peaks, and steaming mugs of glühwein make the Grand Alpine Hotel almost as memorable as the murder itself.

Clever, atmospheric, and entertaining, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel is a worthy tribute to Agatha Christie. Christie fans, as well as lovers of classic locked-room mysteries, are sure to enjoy this one.

‘...one cannot extinguish wickedness with more of the same. It is like a stain, an infection. It only grows…’

4.5 stars rounded up
"High in the Swiss Alps, accessible only by a single, winding railway, stands the luxurious Grand Alpine Hotel. With glorious mountain views and exclusive access to powdery slopes, it draws guests from far and wide.

The notorious actress.
The high-flying politician.
The society wife.
The reckless friend.
The shrewd doctor.

But not everyone is here for a winter holiday."

There are some who appear to have nefarious motives. When a body unexpectedly shows up, the only way out is blocked, trapping everyone with an unidentified killer. Fortunately, Miss Marple is in the shadows observing everything going on until the Swiss police can arrive. But how high will the body count get before the killer can be stopped?

Let me just say that writing the first in a new Miss Marple series is a huge task - and Lucy Foley understood the assignment. She channeled Agatha Christie perfectly! The book takes place in the 1950s and the language is reminiscent of Christie. She created the perfect locked room/closed circuit mystery. I have read most of Foley's novels and this book does not have her signature voice. It feels like an Agatha Christie novel that I found so entertaining and fun to read. Beautifully done in a way Agatha Christie would have been proud of. It is propulsive and I am thoroughly impressed and highly recommend for Agatha Christie fans.

Many thanks to NetGalley, William Morrow and Lucy Foley for the gifted advance reader's copy. All opinions are my own.

EXCERPT: The shadowy figure in the gondola sits with their head thrown back against the rear window; perhaps in awestruck appreciation of the view.
The mechanism grinds to a halt. The doors begin to open. The seated figure does not move.
The attendant peers through the cabin window. Are they asleep? Are they not intending to get out? Perhaps they’ve come up here for the sights and will simply stay put and travel back the way they’ve come. More snow is on the way, after all: a great deal of it.
And yet . . . there’s something odd. A peculiar stillness about the scene. The attendant feels that he is just as alone as he was before the gondola and its occupant emerged through the clouds.
Should he go and see?
He doesn’t want to see.
He’s struck by the sudden impulse (odd; he’s a good Swiss Protestant) to cross himself.
Just as he steps out of his cabin into the freezing air the gondola gives the mechanical shudder that locks it into the final position. This is when the seated figure falls, stiff and inert as a Dresden doll knocked from a mantelpiece, keeling face- first onto the metal floor of the cabin.
For a moment the attendant watches in horror. Then he springs into action. But he knows, even as he hastens along the ice- slick path, that it is no use. The gondola’s passenger is already dead.

ABOUT 'MURDER AT THE GRAND ALPINE HOTEL': High in the Swiss Alps, with glorious mountain views and exclusive access to powdery slopes, the Grand Alpine Hotel draws guests from far and wide.

The notorious actress

The high-flying politician

The inscrutable political wife

The reckless friend

The shrewd doctor

But when a guest enters a gondola alive, only to be found dead at the top of the mountain, it’s clear there’s a killer in their midst.

As tensions rise, and old grudges emerge like cracks in the ice, someone watches from the shadows. An unassuming woman with an extraordinary mind: Miss Marple.

She suspects everyone in the hotel, and she’s right to. For it isn’t just a question of who has a motive, but who’s next…

MY THOUGHTS: ‘I find the actions of human beings are usually far more portentous of coming danger than any natural phenomenon.’

Miss Marple has always been my favorite of the Agatha Christie detectives. I love her ability to fade into the background, to go unnoticed and yet, when she needs to, she has a core of steel beneath that innocuous exterior.

As you can see by my rating, I enjoyed this murder mystery. BUT I had to put out of my mind that this was a Miss Marple mystery because it neither read nor felt like one. Perhaps my expectations were too high on the Miss Marple front.

But if you are looking for an entertaining cozy mystery with plenty of twists, red herrings and a cast of mostly unlikeable characters with a little war crime thrown in for good measure, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel fills the bill nicely.

There is a good cast of narrators (I particularly appreciated that!) but whomever was narrating Jane Marple was a little shrill at times. And one thing Jane Marple never was, was shrill.

A fun but not particularly memorable read.

⭐⭐⭐.9
